newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch could sell 200 tonnes more gold - Rabobank.
newsitem.headline: Dutch could sell 200 tonnes more gold - Rabobank.

text.p: The Dutch central bank, which last week rocked the bullion market with news of a major gold sale, still holds enough to sell a further 200 tonnes from its reserves, an analyst at a leading Dutch bank said on Wednesday.

Monique van Gils of the Economics Research Department at Rabobank said there was no longer any justification for holding extensive gold reserves and predicted further official sales from countries such as Portugal.

"Gold no longer has a significant formal role in the international monetary system and it hardly influences public confidence in the monetary authorities," she wrote in the bank's financial weekly report.
"Taking into account a reasonable contribution to the new European Central Bank, De Nederlandse Bank could, according to our calculations, even sell 200 tonnes of gold more."

The gold market was stunned by news earlier this month that the Dutch sold 300 tonnes of gold during 1996, earning it $3.8 billion in foreign reserves. The sale, some one-fifth of its total gold reserves, still leaves the Dutch sitting on 1,052 tonnes.
That news, coupled with the fear that other central banks may follow suit, has been a major factor behind the gold price tumbling to 3-1/4-year lows this year.
On Wednesday morning, gold was fixed in London at $350.10 an ounce having dipped briefly below the psychologically-important $350 level, its lowest since mid-September 1993.
As news of the Dutch sale hit the market, Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer sought to allay any concerns over further official divestments.
Speaking in his capacity as chairman of the G10 central bank governors' committee, he said then: "For the time being, there is no intention for central banks to sell gold."

But Van Gils on Wednesday pointed to the financial gains for the Dutch authorities in making the move. The central bank said it would earn an extra 250 million guilders a year by investing the foreign currency proceeds of the sale.
"Gold was a bad investment over the past 10 years because the price has declined and gold is not returning interest."
Others banks might be tempted by this argument, she said, singling out Portugal as a prime contender as it holds the largest reserves of gold as a percentage of GDP in the European Union.

Turning back to the Netherlands, Van Gils adds that the country's high coverage ratio would not stop a further bullion sale. By royal decree, the total amount of banknotes and cash accounts has to be at least 50 percent covered by gold and foreign currency reserves.
This ratio is running at 160 percent and, because the book value of gold in reserve is lower than the actual market value, a gold sale will increase this ratio.

However, other analysts have pointed out that the world's large gold holders are unlikely to sell off reserves. They say such a move would be counter-productive as it would undoubtedly undermine the price, angering those with bullion still in their vaults.
The purely financial argument for bullion sales also ignores gold's almost mystical status as an ultimate store of value in times of economic collapse.
